questions.s: Researchers in Karachi want to study whether betel quid and gutka chewing is associated with oral cancer, a relatively rare disease. They have limited time and funds. Which study design is most appropriate?
questions.e: For a rare disease, a case-control study starting from people with oral cancer and comparing past exposure with controls is quick and cheap. A cohort study would need very large numbers followed for years to collect enough cases, and an RCT of a harmful exposure would be unethical.

questions.s: In a cohort study in Lahore, 1,000 smokers and 1,000 non-smokers were followed for 10 years. Lung cancer developed in 30 smokers and 5 non-smokers. What is the relative risk of lung cancer in smokers?
questions.e: Relative risk is the incidence in the exposed divided by the incidence in the unexposed: (30/1,000) / (5/1,000) = 6. The figure 25 is the attributable risk per 1,000 (30 - 5), not the relative risk.

questions.s: A survey measures fasting glucose in 3,000 adults in Hyderabad on a single occasion and reports the proportion who have diabetes. Which measure does this study provide?
questions.e: A cross-sectional survey at one point in time measures the proportion of people who have the condition, which is prevalence. Incidence needs follow-up of a population free of disease to count new cases over time.

questions.s: A trial compares a new oral drug with placebo to reduce stroke. Stroke occurs in 20 % of the placebo group and 15 % of the drug group over 5 years. How many patients must be treated for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
questions.e: Absolute risk reduction is 20 % - 15 % = 5 % (0.05), and the number needed to treat is 1/0.05 = 20. The relative risk reduction is 25 %, which is easily confused with NNT but expresses a proportion, not a number of patients.

questions.s: In a group of 200 people known to have tuberculosis on culture, a new rapid test is positive in 180. What is the sensitivity of the test?
questions.e: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive: 180/200 = 90 %. The 10 % who test negative are false negatives; specificity would need data from people without tuberculosis.

questions.s: Systolic blood pressure in a large healthy adult population is normally distributed with a mean of 120 mmHg and a standard deviation of 10 mmHg. Between which values will about 95 % of the population lie?
questions.e: In a normal distribution about 95 % of values lie within 1.96 (about 2) standard deviations of the mean: 120 ± 20 gives roughly 100 to 140 mmHg. About 68 % lie within 1 SD (110 to 130 mmHg) and 99.7 % within 3 SD.

questions.s: A 9-month-old child in a rural union council in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa develops sudden weakness of the left leg with fever; the leg is floppy and reflexes are absent. Which action is the most important for polio surveillance?
o: Collect two stool samples 24 hours apart within 14 days of onset
Send a throat swab for viral culture
Start a course of intramuscular injections for pain relief
Wait for the 60-day follow-up examination and report only if weakness persists
questions.e: Every case of acute flaccid paralysis in a child under 15 years must be reported immediately and two adequate stool samples collected at least 24 hours apart within 14 days of onset for poliovirus testing. Intramuscular injections should be avoided in a child with possible polio because they can provoke paralysis in the injected limb.

questions.s: A vaccinator in Thatta checks a vial of oral polio vaccine before use. The inner square of the vaccine vial monitor is the same colour as the outer circle. What should she do?
o: Use the vial within the same day
Use it only for children over 1 year
Discard the vial and report it
Put it in the freezer to restore potency
questions.e: Once the inner square matches or is darker than the outer circle, the vial has had too much cumulative heat exposure and must not be used. Freezing does not restore potency of a heat-damaged vaccine.

questions.s: A 2-month-old girl is brought to a BHU with cough. She is alert and feeding, with no chest indrawing or danger signs. Which respiratory rate defines fast breathing in her age group under IMCI?
questions.e: Under IMCI, fast breathing is 50 or more breaths per minute at 2 to 12 months, and 40 or more at 12 months to 5 years. The threshold of 60 or more is used for young infants under 2 months.

questions.s: A community health worker measures mid-upper arm circumference in a 2-year-old child in Tharparkar. The child has no oedema. Which MUAC indicates severe acute malnutrition?
questions.e: For children aged 6 to 59 months, a MUAC below 11.5 cm defines severe acute malnutrition; 11.5 to below 12.5 cm indicates moderate acute malnutrition. Bilateral pitting oedema also defines SAM regardless of MUAC.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man who worked as a stone crusher for 20 years has progressive breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows multiple small nodules in the upper zones with eggshell calcification of hilar nodes. Which infection is he at particular risk of?
questions.e: Silicosis, from inhaling crystalline silica in stone crushing and quarrying, impairs macrophage function and greatly increases the risk of pulmonary tuberculosis. Pneumocystis pneumonia is linked to severe immune suppression such as advanced HIV, not to silica exposure.

questions.s: A district health officer runs a programme of mammography for women aged 50 to 70 years to detect breast cancer before symptoms appear. What level of prevention is this?
questions.e: Secondary prevention detects disease early, before symptoms, so that treatment can improve outcome; screening is the main example. Primary prevention stops disease from starting, as with vaccination, while tertiary prevention reduces disability from established disease.

questions.s: In a trial of a new antihypertensive drug, patients are allocated to drug or placebo by a computer-generated random sequence. What is the main purpose of randomisation?
o: To make the results applicable to all populations and settings
To prevent patients knowing their treatment
To balance known and unknown confounders between groups
questions.e: Random allocation makes the groups similar in both known and unknown prognostic factors, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. Preventing patients knowing their treatment is the purpose of blinding, not randomisation.

questions.s: In a case-control study of oral cleft, 40 of 100 mothers of affected babies and 20 of 100 mothers of healthy babies report taking a certain drug in early pregnancy. What is the odds ratio?
questions.e: Odds of exposure in cases = 40/60 and in controls = 20/80; odds ratio = (40 × 80) / (60 × 20) = 3,200/1,200 ≈ 2.7. The value 2.0 comes from dividing the proportions exposed (40 %/20 %), which is not the correct measure in a case-control study.

questions.s: Mothers of children with leukaemia and mothers of healthy children are asked about X-ray exposure during pregnancy. Mothers of affected children remember exposures much more thoroughly. What type of bias is this?
questions.e: Recall bias occurs when cases remember past exposures differently from controls, typically more thoroughly because they search for a cause; it is a key weakness of case-control studies. Lead-time bias applies to screening, where earlier diagnosis appears to prolong survival.

questions.s: A screening test for diabetes was used in 1,000 adults. Of 100 people with diabetes, 90 tested positive; of 900 without diabetes, 40 tested positive. What is the positive predictive value?
questions.e: PPV is true positives divided by all positives: 90 / (90 + 40) = 69 %. Sensitivity is 90 %, specificity is 860/900 ≈ 96 % and negative predictive value is 860/870 ≈ 99 %, so each distractor is a different property of the same test.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man in Rawalpindi is bitten on the hand by a stray dog that broke the skin and caused bleeding. He has never been vaccinated against rabies. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Wound washing and rabies vaccine only
Observe the dog and start rabies vaccine only if it dies within 10 days
Wound washing, rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin
questions.e: A transdermal bite with bleeding is a WHO category III exposure, needing immediate thorough wound washing, rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound. Waiting to see if the dog dies is not acceptable; the 10-day observation can only guide stopping treatment.

questions.s: The basic reproduction number (R0) of a disease in a fully susceptible population is 5. What minimum proportion of the population must be immune to interrupt transmission (herd immunity threshold)?
questions.e: The herd immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/5 = 0.8, so at least 80 % must be immune. Diseases with a higher R0, such as measles, need a threshold of about 95 %.

questions.s: An EPI cold chain officer suspects a carton of pentavalent vaccine may have frozen during transport. Which test should be done to decide whether it can be used?
o: Potency test at the district store
questions.e: Freezing damages adsorbed vaccines such as pentavalent, hepatitis B and tetanus-containing vaccines; in the shake test, a frozen vial sediments faster than a deliberately frozen control. The vaccine vial monitor shows heat exposure, not freezing.

questions.s: A 6-month-old boy with watery diarrhoea and some dehydration is treated at a BHU with low-osmolarity ORS. Which additional treatment is recommended for 10 to 14 days to reduce the duration and recurrence of diarrhoea?
questions.e: WHO and IMCI recommend zinc supplements for 10 to 14 days in childhood diarrhoea alongside ORS, reducing duration, severity and recurrence. Antimotility drugs such as loperamide are not used in young children, and antibiotics are reserved for bloody diarrhoea or cholera.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl's height-for-age is below -2 SD on the WHO growth standard, while her weight-for-height is normal. What does this indicate?
questions.e: Low height-for-age is stunting and reflects chronic undernutrition and repeated infection over a long period. Low weight-for-height is wasting, which reflects acute malnutrition.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman who has worked in a cotton mill in Faisalabad for many years has chest tightness and cough that are worst on the first day back at work after the weekend and improve as the week goes on. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Byssinosis, from cotton, flax or hemp dust, classically causes chest tightness on the first working day of the week (Monday fever). Farmer's lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis from mouldy hay with fever and breathlessness hours after exposure.

questions.s: Which international conference declared primary health care as the key to achieving health for all?
questions.e: The Declaration of Alma-Ata in 1978 identified primary health care as the key to attaining health for all. The Ottawa Charter (1986) concerns health promotion, and the Astana declaration reaffirmed primary health care rather than first declaring it.

questions.s: A study finds that people who carry matches are more likely to develop lung cancer. When smoking is taken into account, the association disappears. What explains the original association?
questions.e: Smoking is linked to both carrying matches and lung cancer and is not on the causal pathway, so it confounds the association. Effect modification means the strength of an association genuinely differs across subgroups, rather than vanishing after adjustment.

questions.s: The weights of newborns in a district hospital are recorded as a continuous variable. Researchers compare the mean birth weight of babies whose mothers smoked with that of babies whose mothers did not. Which test is most appropriate if the data are normally distributed?
o: Chi-square test of birth weight categories
questions.e: Comparing the means of a continuous, normally distributed variable between two independent groups uses the unpaired (independent samples) t-test. A paired t-test is for two measurements in the same individuals, and chi-square compares proportions.

questions.s: In a village in Badin, 30 infant deaths were recorded in a year in which there were 1,200 live births. What is the infant mortality rate?
questions.e: Infant mortality rate = deaths under 1 year of age / live births in the same year × 1,000 = 30/1,200 × 1,000 = 25 per 1,000 live births. The denominator is live births, not total population or the number of infants alive at the end of the year.

questions.s: After a wedding dinner in Sukkur, 60 of the 200 guests develop vomiting and diarrhoea within 6 hours. What is the attack rate?
questions.e: The attack rate is the number of new cases divided by the population at risk during the outbreak: 60/200 = 30 %. It is an incidence proportion used for short outbreaks with a well-defined exposed group.

questions.s: The annual incidence of a chronic disease in a stable population is 10 per 1,000, and the average duration of the disease is 3 years. Assuming steady state, what is the approximate prevalence?
questions.e: In a steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration = 10 per 1,000 per year × 3 years = 30 per 1,000. Treatments that prolong survival without cure therefore raise prevalence even if incidence is unchanged.

questions.s: In a cohort study, the incidence of lung cancer is 30 per 1,000 among smokers and 5 per 1,000 among non-smokers. What proportion of lung cancer among smokers can be attributed to smoking (attributable risk per cent)?
questions.e: Attributable risk per cent = (incidence in exposed - incidence in unexposed) / incidence in exposed = (30 - 5)/30 ≈ 83 %. The attributable risk itself is 25 per 1,000, and the relative risk is 6.

questions.s: The monthly incomes of 50 households in a Lahore katchi abadi are very skewed, with a few households earning far more than the rest. Which measure best summarises the typical income?
questions.e: The median is not pulled by extreme values, so it represents the typical value in skewed data better than the mean, which is pulled towards the long tail. The range describes spread, not central tendency.

questions.s: A study compares the proportion of children with anaemia in two districts: 120 of 400 children in one and 80 of 400 in the other. Which statistical test is most appropriate to compare these proportions?
questions.e: Comparing proportions of a categorical outcome between independent groups uses the chi-square test. The t-test and analysis of variance compare means of continuous variables.

questions.s: A trial reports that a new drug lowers blood pressure more than an older one, with p = 0.03. What is the correct interpretation of this p value?
o: There is a 3 % probability that the new drug is truly no better than the old drug
With no true difference, a result this extreme would occur about 3 % of the time
The new drug is effective in 97 % of patients
The study has 97 % power to detect a difference
questions.e: The p value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor a measure of how many patients benefit.

questions.s: A sample of 100 adults has a mean haemoglobin of 12.5 g/dL with a standard deviation of 20 g/L (2 g/dL). What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.e: Standard error = SD / √n = 2 / √100 = 2/10 = 0.2 g/dL. The standard deviation describes spread of individual values, while the standard error describes the precision of the sample mean and shrinks as sample size increases.

questions.s: Researchers conclude that a new drug reduces mortality, but in truth it has no effect; the result arose by chance. What type of error is this?
questions.e: A type I (alpha) error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, finding a difference that does not exist; its probability is set by the significance level, often 5 %. A type II (beta) error is failing to detect a real difference, usually because the study is too small.

questions.s: A new rapid test for malaria is used on 1,000 people who do not have malaria on microscopy. The test is negative in 950. What is the specificity?
questions.e: Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative: 950/1,000 = 95 %. The 50 who test positive are false positives (5 % false positive rate).

questions.s: Survival from diagnosis of a cancer appears longer in screened patients than in those diagnosed after symptoms, yet the age at death is the same in both groups. Which bias best explains this?
questions.e: Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier without delaying death, so survival from diagnosis seems longer. Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially detects slow-growing tumours with better prognosis.

questions.s: A test has a sensitivity of 90 % and a specificity of 80 %. What is its positive likelihood ratio?
questions.e: Positive likelihood ratio = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.9/0.2 = 4.5, meaning a positive result is 4.5 times more likely in someone with the disease than without. The negative likelihood ratio is (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = 0.1/0.8 = 0.125.

questions.s: Health planners are deciding whether to start a national screening programme for a condition. Which feature is an essential criterion for a screening programme?
o: The condition must be rare in the population so that few people need follow-up
An accepted treatment must exist for patients found to have the condition
The condition must have a short latent period
questions.e: Classic Wilson-Jungner criteria require that the condition is an important health problem, with a recognisable latent or early stage, a suitable acceptable test and an accepted treatment for those detected. A long, not short, latent period is needed so there is time to detect disease early, and no test is 100 % sensitive.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy lives with his father, who has just been diagnosed with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. The child is well and active TB has been excluded. What is the most appropriate management for the child?
o: Repeat chest X-ray in 6 months only
questions.e: WHO recommends tuberculosis preventive treatment (for example isoniazid) for household contacts under 5 years once active disease is excluded, because young children are at high risk of severe TB. Full four-drug treatment is reserved for active disease, and BCG revaccination is not recommended.

questions.s: Dengue cases rise every year after the monsoon in Rawalpindi. Which community measure best targets the main vector?
o: Removing water collected in tyres, pots and coolers around homes
Spraying larvicide in the marshes and swamps on the outskirts of the city
Using untreated nets only at night
questions.e: Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti, a day-biting mosquito that breeds in clean water in containers such as tyres, flower pots, water tanks and coolers, so source reduction around homes is the key measure. Marshes and rice fields are breeding sites for Anopheles and Culex rather than Aedes, and night-time nets protect poorly against day biters.

questions.s: A district health officer is notified of several cases of acute watery diarrhoea in one neighbourhood. After confirming the reports, which step comes next in an outbreak investigation?
o: Establish a case definition and confirm that an outbreak exists
Publish a report of the outbreak
Implement final control measures and formally close the investigation
Start a randomised trial of treatments
questions.e: Early steps in an outbreak investigation are to verify the diagnosis, confirm that cases exceed the expected number, and establish a case definition to find and count cases; control measures are started as soon as possible but are refined as data emerge. Writing the final report comes at the end.

questions.s: At a vaccination session at a BHU, which vaccine is given intradermally at birth over the left upper arm?
questions.e: BCG is given intradermally, usually over the left deltoid, at birth to protect against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis such as miliary TB and TB meningitis. Hepatitis B birth dose is given intramuscularly.

questions.s: In Pakistan's EPI schedule, a child receives pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. Which diseases does this vaccine protect against?
o: Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and Hib
Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, polio and measles
Measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis B and varicella
Tuberculosis, diphtheria, tetanus, polio and hepatitis B
questions.e: Pentavalent vaccine combines DTP with hepatitis B and Hib antigens. Polio is covered separately by OPV and IPV, and measles by the measles-containing vaccine given at 9 and 15 months.

questions.s: Which vaccine used in the routine immunisation programme is the most sensitive to heat and so is stored at the coldest temperature at central and provincial stores?
questions.e: Oral polio vaccine is the most heat-sensitive EPI vaccine and is stored frozen at central and provincial levels. Tetanus toxoid, hepatitis B and pentavalent vaccines are damaged by freezing and must be kept at 2 to 8 °C.

questions.s: A mother delivers a healthy baby. She plans to breastfeed only and asks whether this will prevent pregnancy. Under which conditions is the lactational amenorrhoea method reliable?
o: Baby under 6 months, fully or nearly fully breastfed, and periods not returned
Baby under 12 months, mother breastfeeds at least twice a day, any menstrual pattern
Baby under 6 months, any feeding pattern, with periods not returned
Any age of baby if the mother is not menstruating
questions.e: LAM is about 98 % effective only if all three conditions hold: periods have not returned, the baby is fully or nearly fully breastfed, and the baby is under 6 months. Once any condition changes, another method is needed.

questions.s: A baby born at 34 weeks weighing 1.7 kg in a THQ hospital is stable and breathing well. There is no functioning incubator. Which intervention best keeps him warm and reduces neonatal mortality?
o: Wrapping in several blankets in a separate cot
Placing the cot near a heater
Delaying the first feed until warm
questions.e: Kangaroo mother care, with continuous skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breastfeeding, keeps stable low birth weight babies warm and reduces mortality and infection. Delaying feeds increases the risk of hypoglycaemia and does not help temperature.

questions.s: How is the maternal mortality ratio expressed?
o: Maternal deaths per 1,000 women of reproductive age
questions.e: The maternal mortality ratio is the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in the same period. The maternal mortality rate uses women of reproductive age as the denominator instead.

questions.s: For how long does WHO recommend exclusive breastfeeding for infants?
questions.e: WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then nutritionally adequate complementary foods with continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond. Introducing other foods or water earlier increases the risk of diarrhoea and reduces breast milk intake.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy with severe acute malnutrition has a good appetite, no medical complications and no oedema. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Outpatient treatment with ready-to-use therapeutic food
Admission to a stabilisation centre for F-75 therapeutic milk feeds
questions.e: Children with uncomplicated SAM who pass the appetite test are treated as outpatients in community-based programmes with ready-to-use therapeutic food. Admission and F-75 are for complicated SAM, for example with poor appetite or medical complications, and albumin is not used.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man who has worked in a textile weaving unit for many years has bilateral hearing loss. Audiometry shows a dip in hearing threshold centred at 4,000 Hz. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Noise-induced hearing loss is a bilateral sensorineural loss with a characteristic notch around 4 kHz. Presbycusis causes gradually sloping high-frequency loss without a notch, and otosclerosis is a conductive loss.

questions.s: A 9-month-old girl attends a vaccination session in Quetta with a mild cold and a temperature of 37.6 °C. She is due her first measles-rubella vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Postpone all vaccines until she has been well for 4 weeks
Give only oral polio vaccine today
Give a paracetamol course and vaccinate in 2 weeks
questions.e: Minor illness such as a cold or low-grade fever is not a contraindication to vaccination, and delaying leaves the child unprotected and risks a missed opportunity. Vaccination is postponed only for moderate or severe acute illness or genuine contraindications.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends antenatal care at 20 weeks at a rural health centre. She has no record of previous tetanus vaccination. What is recommended to prevent neonatal tetanus?
o: Two doses of Td vaccine 4 weeks apart, the second at least 2 weeks before delivery
A single dose of tetanus immunoglobulin to the mother at delivery and to the baby at birth
Tetanus vaccine for the baby at birth
No vaccine in pregnancy; vaccinate after delivery
questions.e: An unvaccinated pregnant woman needs at least two doses of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine 4 weeks apart, the second at least 2 weeks before delivery, so protective antibodies cross the placenta to the baby. Tetanus vaccine is not given to newborns, and clean delivery and cord care are also essential.

questions.s: In Pakistan, children aged 6 to 59 months receive high-dose vitamin A every 6 months during campaigns. Which outcome is this mainly intended to reduce?
questions.e: Vitamin A supplementation in deficient populations reduces all-cause child mortality, largely by reducing deaths from measles and diarrhoea, as well as preventing xerophthalmia. It has no meaningful effect on iron deficiency anaemia or obesity.

questions.s: A 1-year-old child has been fully assessed: weight-for-height is below -3 SD on the WHO standard and there is no oedema. MUAC is 12.0 cm. How should this child be classified?
o: Moderate acute malnutrition, because MUAC is 11.5 cm or more
Normal nutrition, because MUAC is above 11.5 cm
questions.e: Severe acute malnutrition is defined by any of weight-for-height below -3 SD, MUAC below 11.5 cm or bilateral pitting oedema; meeting one criterion is enough. The MUAC alone would suggest moderate malnutrition, but the weight-for-height places the child in the severe category.

questions.s: A town water supply in Sindh is chlorinated. To make sure the water is safe from bacterial contamination when it reaches homes, what should be measured at the end of the distribution system?
questions.e: Detecting free residual chlorine (around 0.2 to 0.5 mg/L) at the tap shows that enough chlorine was added to satisfy the demand and still protect against recontamination. Hardness and dissolved solids affect taste and acceptability but do not indicate microbiological safety.

questions.s: Several adults in a village in southern Punjab who drink water from shallow hand pumps have raindrop-like pigmentation of the trunk and thick keratoses on the palms and soles. Which contaminant is most likely?
questions.e: Chronic arsenic ingestion from groundwater causes raindrop hyper- and hypopigmentation, palmoplantar keratoses and an increased risk of skin, lung and bladder cancer; parts of Punjab and Sindh have high groundwater arsenic. Fluoride causes dental and skeletal fluorosis, and nitrate causes methaemoglobinaemia in infants.

questions.s: A Lady Health Worker serves households in a rural area of Punjab. Which is part of her standard role?
o: Performing caesarean sections for obstructed labour at home in the community
Counselling on family planning and visiting newborns at home
questions.e: Lady Health Workers provide community-based primary care: family planning counselling and supplies, antenatal and postnatal advice, newborn home visits, growth monitoring, immunisation promotion and treatment of minor illness. Surgical and specialist care is delivered at hospital level.

questions.s: A 32-year-old bus driver in Lahore has poorly controlled epilepsy with recent seizures. He refuses to stop driving or inform his employer despite repeated advice from his doctor. What is the most appropriate step for the doctor?
o: Do nothing because confidentiality is absolute
Tell him first, then disclose only what is needed to the relevant authority
Tell his family and neighbours so that they can persuade him to stop driving
Stop treating him until he agrees to stop driving
questions.e: Confidentiality may be breached when there is a serious risk of harm to others; the doctor should tell the patient first and then disclose only the necessary information to the relevant authority. Telling family and neighbours is an unjustified disclosure, and withdrawing care harms the patient.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with full mental capacity refuses a blood transfusion after a road traffic accident, understanding that he may die. Which ethical principle requires the team to respect his refusal?
questions.e: Autonomy means that a competent adult has the right to make informed decisions about his own care, including refusing life-saving treatment. Beneficence (acting in the patient's best interest) does not override a capacitous refusal.

questions.s: Before a 55-year-old woman has an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon obtains her consent. Which element is essential for this consent to be valid?
o: The consent form is signed by her husband
She is informed of the nature, benefits, material risks and alternatives
The procedure is explained only in medical terminology
She is told that refusing will mean she can no longer be treated at that hospital
questions.e: Valid consent requires that a competent patient is given adequate information about the procedure, benefits, material risks and alternatives in understandable language, and agrees voluntarily. A spouse cannot consent for a capacitous adult, and any threat or pressure makes consent invalid.

questions.s: A study compares average salt intake and stroke mortality across 30 countries and finds a strong positive correlation. A researcher concludes that individuals who eat more salt are more likely to die of stroke. What is the main problem with this conclusion?
questions.e: Ecological studies use group-level data, so associations between populations cannot be assumed to apply to individuals; doing so is the ecological fallacy. Recall bias affects individual-level studies that rely on memory of past exposure, such as case-control studies.

questions.s: In a trial of a new analgesic, neither the patients nor the doctors assessing pain know who received the drug and who received placebo. What is the main purpose of this?
o: To ensure the groups are comparable at baseline
To reduce bias in reporting and assessing outcomes
To allow analysis by intention to treat
questions.e: Double blinding prevents knowledge of the allocation from influencing how patients report symptoms and how assessors record outcomes, reducing performance and detection bias. Comparability at baseline is achieved by randomisation, not blinding.

questions.s: In a randomised trial, some patients allocated to a new drug stopped taking it and some in the control group obtained it elsewhere. The investigators analyse every patient in the group to which they were originally randomised. What is this approach called?
questions.e: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps patients in their randomised groups regardless of what they actually received, preserving the benefits of randomisation and reflecting real-world effectiveness. Per-protocol analysis includes only those who followed the protocol and can reintroduce bias.

questions.s: A doctor in Islamabad wants the strongest available evidence on whether a treatment reduces mortality. Which source usually provides the highest level of evidence?
o: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
questions.e: A well-conducted systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials pools all relevant trials and sits at the top of the usual hierarchy of evidence. Cohort studies are observational and more prone to confounding, and expert opinion is the lowest level.

questions.s: Hand-washing rates among nurses in a hospital ward rise sharply during the week when they know infection control staff are observing them, then fall back afterwards. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.e: The Hawthorne effect is a change in behaviour because people know they are being studied or watched. Regression to the mean is the statistical tendency of extreme measurements to be closer to average when repeated.

questions.s: Investigators recruit 5,000 healthy adults in Peshawar, record their diet, smoking and physical activity, and follow them for 15 years for heart disease, stroke and cancer. Which is a key advantage of this design?
o: It is ideal for very rare diseases
It can measure incidence of several outcomes
questions.e: A prospective cohort study measures exposure before outcomes occur, allowing direct calculation of incidence and relative risk for several outcomes. It is slow and expensive, unsuitable for rare diseases, and still prone to confounding because exposure is not randomised.

questions.s: In a cohort of 600 brick-kiln workers, 300 were exposed to heavy dust and 300 were not. Chronic bronchitis developed in 18 exposed and 6 unexposed workers. What is the relative risk?
questions.e: Relative risk = (18/300) / (6/300) = 0.06/0.02 = 3, so exposed workers have three times the risk. The difference in incidence (0.04, or 4 per 100) is the attributable risk.

questions.s: In a case-control study of hepatocellular carcinoma, 30 of 50 cases and 10 of 50 controls had a history of unsafe injections. What is the odds ratio?
questions.e: Odds ratio = (exposed cases × unexposed controls) / (unexposed cases × exposed controls) = (30 × 40)/(20 × 10) = 1,200/200 = 6. Dividing the proportions exposed (60 %/20 %) gives 3, which is not the odds ratio.

questions.s: In a trial, 10 % of patients given placebo and 6 % given a new drug had a myocardial infarction over 3 years. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one infarction?
questions.e: The absolute risk reduction is 10 % - 6 % = 4 % (0.04), so NNT = 1/0.04 = 25 patients treated for 3 years to prevent one infarction. The relative risk reduction (40 %) is a proportion and must not be confused with NNT.

questions.s: In a survey of 2,500 schoolchildren in Mardan on a single day, 50 had active scabies. What is the point prevalence?
questions.e: Point prevalence = existing cases at one point in time / population examined = 50/2,500 = 2 %. Prevalence includes all existing cases, both new and old.

questions.s: A village has 1,050 adults, of whom 50 already have hypertension at the start of a year. During the year, 20 new cases are diagnosed. What is the one-year cumulative incidence of hypertension?
questions.e: Cumulative incidence = new cases / population at risk at the start; the 50 who already have hypertension are not at risk, so it is 20/1,000 = 2.0 %. Using the whole population of 1,050 as denominator wrongly gives 1.9 %.

questions.s: Following a school lunch in Mirpur Khas, 45 of the 150 pupils who ate chicken rice developed vomiting, compared with very few who did not eat it. What is the attack rate among those who ate chicken rice?
questions.e: Attack rate = 45/150 = 30 %. Comparing food-specific attack rates between those who ate and did not eat each item identifies the likely vehicle of a foodborne outbreak.

questions.s: The number of days of hospital stay for six patients is 3, 5, 7, 8, 12 and 40. What is the median length of stay?
questions.e: With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: (7 + 8)/2 = 7.5 days. The mean is 12.5 days, pulled upwards by the extreme value of 40.

questions.s: A random sample of 400 adults has a mean systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg with a standard deviation of 20 mmHg. What is the approximate 95 % confidence interval for the population mean?
questions.e: Standard error = 20/√400 = 1 mmHg, so the 95 % CI is 140 ± 1.96 × 1 ≈ 138 to 142 mmHg. The range 100 to 180 mmHg (mean ± 2 SD) describes where about 95 % of individual values lie, not the precision of the mean.

questions.s: A small trial of 40 patients finds no significant difference between two antihypertensive drugs, although a real difference exists. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Type I error due to multiple testing
Type II error due to low power
questions.e: Failing to detect a true difference is a type II error, most often because the sample is too small, giving low power. A type I error is a false positive finding.

questions.s: A study of 200 adults finds a correlation coefficient (r) of -0.8 between hours of weekly exercise and fasting triglycerides. What does this indicate?
o: That exercise has been proven to lower triglycerides
questions.e: An r of -0.8 shows a strong inverse linear association: as exercise increases, triglycerides tend to decrease. Correlation alone does not prove causation, as confounders may explain the association.

questions.s: Patients rate their pain after surgery as none, mild, moderate or severe. What type of data is this?
questions.e: Ordinal data have categories with a natural order but unequal or unknown intervals between them. Nominal data, such as blood group, have categories with no order.

questions.s: Fasting glucose is measured in 30 patients with diabetes before and after 3 months of a lifestyle programme. The differences are normally distributed. Which test is most appropriate to compare the before and after means?
questions.e: Two measurements on the same individuals are compared with a paired t-test, which analyses the within-person differences. The independent samples t-test assumes two separate groups and ignores the pairing.

questions.s: A new test for hepatitis C was evaluated in 200 people. Of 50 with infection, 45 tested positive; of 150 without infection, 120 tested negative. What is the specificity?
questions.e: Specificity = true negatives / all without disease = 120/150 = 80 %. Sensitivity is 45/50 = 90 %, PPV is 45/75 = 60 % and NPV is 120/125 = 96 %.

questions.s: A test with 99 % sensitivity and 95 % specificity is used to screen 10,000 people for a condition with a prevalence of 1 %. Approximately what is the positive predictive value?
questions.e: Of 100 people with the condition, 99 test positive; of 9,900 without it, 5 % (495) are false positives, so PPV = 99/(99 + 495) ≈ 17 %. Even an excellent test has a low PPV when the condition is rare.

questions.s: A screening test is moved from a general population clinic to a specialist clinic where the disease is much more common. The test's sensitivity and specificity are unchanged. What happens to its positive predictive value?
questions.e: Predictive values depend on prevalence: as prevalence rises, true positives rise relative to false positives, so PPV increases while NPV falls. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence.

questions.s: In a screening programme, people with a positive first test are given a second, different test, and only those positive on both are labelled as having the disease. Compared with either test alone, what is the effect of this approach?
questions.e: Sequential (series) testing requires both tests to be positive, which reduces false positives (higher specificity) but misses more true cases (lower sensitivity). Parallel testing, where a positive on either counts, increases sensitivity instead.

questions.s: A laboratory lowers the fasting glucose cut-off used to label a screening test as positive for diabetes. What will happen to the test's performance?
questions.e: Lowering the cut-off classifies more people as positive, catching more true cases (higher sensitivity) but also more false positives (lower specificity). There is a trade-off between the two when changing a cut-off on a continuous test.

questions.s: A doctor wants a test that, if negative, reliably rules out a serious disease. Which property of the test is most important?
questions.e: A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result effectively rules the disease out (SnNout). A highly specific test is better for ruling in disease when positive (SpPin).

questions.s: A child living in a large family compound in Lyari, Karachi, develops measles. Of the 40 susceptible contacts living in the compound, 10 develop measles within one incubation period. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.e: Secondary attack rate = new cases among susceptible contacts / number of susceptible contacts = 10/40 = 25 %; the primary case is excluded from both numerator and denominator. It measures how readily a disease spreads among contacts.

questions.s: Healthy travellers who were exposed to a passenger with a dangerous infectious disease are kept apart and observed for the length of the incubation period. What is this measure called?
questions.e: Quarantine restricts the movement of healthy people who have been exposed, for up to the longest incubation period, to see whether they develop disease. Isolation separates people who are already ill or infected.

questions.s: A cook at a hotel in Hyderabad is found to be the source of several typhoid cases. He had typhoid two years ago and is well, but Salmonella Typhi is repeatedly isolated from his stool. Where does the organism most commonly persist in such carriers?
questions.e: Chronic typhoid carriers usually harbour Salmonella Typhi in the gallbladder, often with gallstones, and excrete it in stool for over a year. Carriers must be excluded from food handling until cleared.

questions.s: A nurse who has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B has a needle-stick injury from a patient known to be HBsAg positive. After washing the wound, what is the most appropriate prophylaxis?
o: Hepatitis B vaccine alone after 6 months
Antiviral therapy with tenofovir for 28 days
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the first vaccine dose promptly
questions.e: An unvaccinated person exposed to an HBsAg-positive source should receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and start the hepatitis B vaccine course as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours. Immunoglobulin alone gives only short-term protection, and delayed vaccination misses the window for prevention.

questions.s: Malaria is endemic in parts of Balochistan and Sindh. Which measure most effectively protects people while they sleep from the mosquito that transmits malaria?
questions.e: Anopheles mosquitoes bite mainly at night, so sleeping under long-lasting insecticide-treated nets reduces bites and malaria transmission. Covering water containers mainly targets Aedes, the dengue vector.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy from a rural area in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer with a raised edge on his cheek for 3 months. Several children in the area have similar lesions. Which vector is responsible?
questions.e: Cutaneous leishmaniasis, common in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, is transmitted by the bite of the female phlebotomine sandfly and causes chronic painless ulcers on exposed skin. Reduviid bugs transmit Chagas disease and tsetse flies sleeping sickness, which are not found in Pakistan.

questions.s: In an outbreak of measles, the attack rate was 20 % among unvaccinated children and 4 % among vaccinated children. What is the vaccine efficacy?
questions.e: Vaccine efficacy = (attack rate in unvaccinated - attack rate in vaccinated) / attack rate in unvaccinated = (20 - 4)/20 = 80 %. The 16 % is the absolute reduction in attack rate, not the efficacy.

questions.s: At a health facility, vaccines such as pentavalent, measles-rubella and tetanus-diphtheria are kept in an ice-lined refrigerator. Within which temperature range should they be stored?
questions.e: At health facility level, routine vaccines are stored at +2 to +8 °C; freeze-sensitive vaccines such as pentavalent and Td are damaged below 0 °C. Freezer temperatures of -15 to -25 °C are used only for OPV at higher-level stores.

questions.s: Pakistan uses oral polio vaccine in mass campaigns alongside inactivated polio vaccine in routine immunisation. What is the main advantage of oral polio vaccine for interrupting wild poliovirus transmission?
o: It induces strong intestinal mucosal immunity
It is given by injection, ensuring an accurate dose
questions.e: OPV replicates in the gut and induces mucosal IgA, reducing faecal shedding and person-to-person spread of wild poliovirus. Its rare drawbacks are vaccine-associated paralysis and vaccine-derived virus, which IPV does not cause.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant asks to receive all vaccines she missed as a child. Which vaccine should not be given during pregnancy?
questions.e: Live attenuated vaccines such as MMR are avoided in pregnancy because of the theoretical risk to the fetus, and pregnancy should be avoided for a month after vaccination. Td, hepatitis B and inactivated influenza vaccines are safe in pregnancy.

questions.s: A baby is born at a THQ hospital to a mother whose hepatitis B status is unknown. When should the hepatitis B birth dose ideally be given?
o: Only after the mother's test result is available
questions.e: The hepatitis B birth dose should be given as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, to prevent mother-to-child transmission, which carries a high risk of chronic infection. Waiting for the mother's result delays protection.

questions.s: Several infants vaccinated by the same vaccinator develop painful, hot, pus-filled swellings at the injection site within a week. What is the most likely cause of this adverse event following immunisation?
o: An immunisation programme error such as non-sterile technique
A coincidental event unrelated to vaccination
questions.e: A cluster of bacterial abscesses linked to one vaccinator suggests an immunisation error, such as reuse of syringes or a contaminated multi-dose vial, which must be investigated and corrected. A vaccine product reaction would be expected across vaccinators using the same batch.

questions.s: In a district with 20,000 live births in a year, 6 women died from pregnancy-related causes during pregnancy or within 42 days of delivery. What is the maternal mortality ratio?
questions.e: Maternal mortality ratio = maternal deaths / live births × 100,000 = 6/20,000 × 100,000 = 30 per 100,000 live births. Maternal deaths are those during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end from causes related to or aggravated by pregnancy.

questions.s: In a district hospital, there were 1,600 live births in a year and 24 babies died within the first 28 days of life. What is the neonatal mortality rate?
questions.e: Neonatal mortality rate = deaths in the first 28 days / live births × 1,000 = 24/1,600 × 1,000 = 15 per 1,000. Early neonatal deaths are those in the first 7 days.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy with fever and cough is brought to a BHU. Under IMCI, which finding is a general danger sign needing urgent referral?
o: Not able to drink or breastfeed
questions.e: IMCI general danger signs are inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, and lethargy or unconsciousness; any one requires urgent referral after pre-referral treatment. Short-duration fever and cough are assessed further but are not danger signs on their own.

questions.s: A primigravida in active labour at an RHC is monitored with a partograph. Her cervical dilatation plot crosses to the right of the alert line. What does this indicate?
o: Labour is slower than expected and needs closer assessment or referral
questions.e: Crossing the alert line means cervical dilatation is slower than 1 cm per hour; at a peripheral facility this is the signal to refer to a facility able to manage complications, and at the action line active intervention is needed. The partograph does not itself confirm fetal distress, which is judged from fetal heart rate and liquor.

questions.s: A district health officer in Punjab wants a single figure estimating the average number of children a woman would bear over her reproductive life if current age-specific fertility rates continued. Which indicator should be used?
questions.e: The total fertility rate is the sum of the age-specific fertility rates across the reproductive years and estimates the average number of children per woman, making it the best single measure of family size. The general fertility rate is live births per 1,000 women aged 15-49 in a year, and the net reproduction rate counts only daughters who survive to replace their mothers.

questions.s: A district is reporting its perinatal mortality rate. Which deaths are included in the numerator?
o: Stillbirths and early neonatal deaths in the first 7 days
All deaths in the first 28 days
All deaths under 1 year of age
questions.e: Perinatal mortality includes stillbirths (late fetal deaths) plus early neonatal deaths in the first week of life, expressed per 1,000 total births. Deaths in the first 28 days make up the neonatal mortality rate instead.

questions.s: A 2-year-old child's weight-for-height is below -2 SD of the WHO median, while height-for-age is normal. What does this indicate?
questions.e: Low weight-for-height is wasting, a sign of acute undernutrition, often from recent illness or food shortage. Stunting is low height-for-age and reflects chronic undernutrition.

questions.s: An 18-month-old girl with severe acute malnutrition and pneumonia is admitted to a stabilisation centre. She has no appetite. Which approach to feeding is recommended during the initial stabilisation phase?
o: Start ready-to-use therapeutic food at full energy intake
Give F-100 with added iron from day 1
Start F-75 in small frequent feeds without added iron
Withhold feeds for 24 hours and give intravenous fluids
questions.e: In complicated SAM, stabilisation uses F-75, which is low in protein and sodium, in small frequent feeds day and night to prevent hypoglycaemia and hypothermia; iron is withheld until the rehabilitation phase. Withholding feeds risks hypoglycaemia, and high-energy feeds early can precipitate refeeding problems and heart failure.

questions.s: A mother asks when she should start giving her exclusively breastfed baby other foods in addition to breast milk. What should she be advised?
questions.e: Complementary foods should be introduced at 6 months, when breast milk alone no longer meets energy and micronutrient needs, while breastfeeding continues to 2 years or beyond. Starting before 6 months increases infections and reduces breast milk intake.

questions.s: Which nutritional deficiency is recognised as the world's most common preventable cause of intellectual disability?
questions.e: Iodine deficiency in pregnancy and early childhood impairs brain development and is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability; severe deficiency causes cretinism. Vitamin A deficiency is the leading preventable cause of childhood blindness.

questions.s: A Lady Health Worker plots a 10-month-old boy's monthly weights on his growth chart. His weight has stayed the same for 3 months, so his line has become flat and is moving away from the reference curves. What does this indicate?
o: Normal growth pattern for his age
questions.e: A flat or falling growth line indicates growth faltering, which should prompt assessment of feeding and illness even if the weight is still within the normal range. Stunting refers to low length-for-age and cannot be judged from weight alone.

questions.s: Pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Pakistan are given daily iron and folic acid tablets. What is the main purpose?
o: Prevent maternal anaemia and reduce low birth weight
questions.e: Daily iron and folic acid in pregnancy reduce maternal anaemia and iron deficiency and are associated with lower rates of low birth weight; folic acid around conception also prevents neural tube defects. They do not prevent pre-eclampsia or goitre.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has worked for 25 years breaking up old ships at the Gadani shipyard. He has progressive breathlessness, finger clubbing and bilateral basal crackles; chest X-ray shows pleural plaques. Which cancer is he at particular risk of?
questions.e: Shipbreaking exposes workers to asbestos insulation; asbestosis causes basal fibrosis and pleural plaques, and asbestos greatly increases the risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer. Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride, and bladder cancer to aromatic amines in dye industries.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man who recycles car batteries in a small workshop in Lahore has abdominal colic, constipation, anaemia and weakness of wrist extension. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Battery recycling causes lead exposure, with colic, anaemia with basophilic stippling and motor neuropathy such as wrist drop; blood lead level confirms it. Mercury and arsenic produce different syndromes and are not linked to battery work.

questions.s: A 40-year-old construction labourer in Jacobabad collapses at work in June. He is confused, his skin is hot and dry, and his core temperature is 41.5 °C. What is the most important immediate action?
o: Give a large volume of oral water while he lies in the sun
Rapid cooling, for example with cool water and fanning
questions.e: Heat stroke is a core temperature above about 40 °C with CNS dysfunction; rapid cooling by evaporation, cool water immersion or ice packs is life-saving. Antipyretics such as paracetamol do not work because the hypothalamic set point is not raised.

questions.s: A family in Quetta is found drowsy with headache and vomiting one winter morning after sleeping in a closed room with a gas heater burning all night. Pulse oximetry reads 98 %. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: High-flow oxygen through a non-rebreather mask
Observation because oxygen saturation is normal
questions.e: Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with high-flow 100 % oxygen, which shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin; carboxyhaemoglobin level is measured on co-oximetry. Standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.s: During floods in Sindh, families have no access to treated water. Which simple household method reliably makes drinking water microbiologically safe?
o: Bringing it to a rolling boil
Filtering through a clean cloth only
Adding a pinch of table salt
questions.e: Bringing water to a rolling boil kills bacteria, viruses and parasites and is the most reliable household method; chlorination is an alternative. Cloth filtration removes some particles and copepods but does not make water free of bacteria.

questions.s: After giving an injection in a busy outpatient department, what is the safest way for a nurse to dispose of the used needle and syringe?
o: Recap the needle with both hands, then discard in a bin
Place it immediately in a puncture-proof sharps container without recapping
Leave it on the tray for later collection
questions.e: Used sharps should go immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use, without recapping, bending or breaking, to prevent needle-stick injuries. Two-handed recapping is a common cause of injury among health workers.

questions.s: A patient with chest pain is first seen at a BHU and then referred upward through the public sector system. Which sequence shows the usual referral pathway from first-level care to the highest district facility?
questions.e: In Pakistan's district health system, Basic Health Units are first-level facilities, Rural Health Centres provide a wider range of services, then Tehsil Headquarter and District Headquarter hospitals provide secondary care. Tertiary teaching hospitals sit above the district level.

questions.s: Health planners want a single measure that combines years of life lost from premature death and years lived with disability to compare the burden of different diseases. Which measure should they use?
questions.e: The DALY combines years of life lost to premature mortality and years lived with disability, so fatal and non-fatal conditions can be compared. Crude death rate and case fatality rate capture only deaths.

questions.s: In a community survey, a doctor finds that many people with hypertension are unaware of it and only a small proportion have been diagnosed and treated. Which concept describes this situation?
questions.e: The iceberg phenomenon describes how diagnosed cases are only the visible tip, while a large hidden mass of undiagnosed, subclinical cases lies beneath; screening aims to uncover this hidden part. Herd immunity relates to indirect protection from immunity in a population.

questions.s: A district hospital has one remaining ICU bed and two patients who need it. The team decides using clear, consistent medical criteria applied to everyone, not on wealth or connections. Which ethical principle is mainly being applied?
questions.e: Justice concerns fair distribution of scarce resources using consistent and relevant criteria. Autonomy refers to respecting a competent patient's own decisions about their care.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man is refusing surgery for a hip fracture. To decide whether he has capacity to make this decision, what should the doctor assess?
o: Whether his decision agrees with medical advice
Whether he can understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a choice
Whether his family agree with his decision
Whether he has a psychiatric diagnosis
questions.e: Capacity is decision-specific: the person must understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, and communicate a decision. An unwise decision, family disagreement or a diagnosis alone does not mean a person lacks capacity.

questions.s: An unconscious 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a ruptured spleen and no relatives present. What is the most appropriate approach to consent for emergency laparotomy?
o: Wait until a relative can be contacted to sign consent
Proceed with life-saving surgery in his best interests
Obtain consent from the police officer who brought him
Delay surgery until he regains consciousness
questions.e: In an emergency, when a patient lacks capacity and delay would risk life or serious harm, doctors may give necessary treatment in the patient's best interests without consent. Police officers cannot consent on a patient's behalf, and waiting for relatives or recovery could be fatal.
